content: The tibia is the larger of the two bones located in the lower leg beneath the knee in vertebrates. In human anatomy, the tibia, also referred to as the shin bone, is positioned medially (towards the midline of the body) and anteriorly (towards the front) relative to the fibula, the other bone in the lower leg. It is the second-longest bone in the human body, with the femur being the longest. The tibia forms joints with the femur and patella at its superior end, with the fibula on its lateral side, and with the ankle at its inferior end. In males, the tibia is oriented vertically and runs parallel to the tibia on the opposite side of the body. In females, however, the tibia has a slightly oblique orientation, angling downward and laterally. This difference compensates for the greater obliquity of the femur in females. The tibia has a prismoid shape. It is wider at its upper end, where it contributes to the knee joint, narrows in its lower third, and then slightly widens again at its lower end. The tibia is connected to the fibula by an interosseous membrane, which forms a type of joint known as a syndesmosis. The arterial blood supply to the tibia comes from two primary sources. The main source is the nutrient artery, while additional blood supply is provided by periosteal vessels that originate from the anterior tibial artery.
